question: Who had more impact on the court: Michael Jordan in 1990-91 or LeBron James in 2014-15?
answer:
# On-Court Impact Review

## Answer

**My judgement: I lean toward Michael Jordan.**

**Criterion:** Evaluating on-court impact through direct offensive production, shooting efficiency, and defensive event proxies.

**Decisive reason:** Michael Jordan generated superior scoring volume and true shooting percentages in both the regular season and playoffs, alongside higher defensive event rates such as steals and blocks per 36 minutes, supporting a provisional preference under an observed-contribution lens. [Evidence](https://stats.nba.com/stats/playercareerstats?PlayerID=893&PerMode=Totals&LeagueID=00) [Evidence](https://stats.nba.com/stats/playercareerstats?PlayerID=2544&PerMode=Totals&LeagueID=00)

**Strongest counterargument:** LeBron James exhibited higher assist production per 36 minutes and greater defensive rebounding volume in the regular season, reflecting strong secondary creation and board work. This does not overturn Michael Jordan's advantage because Michael Jordan maintained a decisive edge in scoring efficiency and defensive disruption metrics. [Evidence](https://stats.nba.com/stats/playercareerstats?PlayerID=893&PerMode=Totals&LeagueID=00) [Evidence](https://stats.nba.com/stats/playercareerstats?PlayerID=2544&PerMode=Totals&LeagueID=00)

**Why this judgement:** Choosing Michael Jordan prioritizes high-volume scoring efficiency and defensive event creation over LeBron James's higher assist generation and ball security trade-offs.

**What could change it:** Additional historical on/off team data or tracking metrics for the left player could reverse this preference if team context demonstrates a significantly larger net impact.

## Dimension findings

- **Offense and era:** Michael Jordan leads the selected measures across the requested phases.
- **Playmaking and ball security:** The indicators disagree; one player does not dominate all selected measures.
- **Defensive evidence:** Regular Season: Michael Jordan has the higher steals per 36 minutes; Regular Season: Michael Jordan has the higher blocks per 36 minutes; Regular Season: LeBron James has the higher defensive rebounds per 36 minutes; Playoffs: Michael Jordan has the higher steals per 36 minutes; Playoffs: Michael Jordan has the higher blocks per 36 minutes; Playoffs: LeBron James has the higher defensive rebounds per 36 minutes. Activity indicators do not settle individual defense.
- **Team on/off context:** Regular Season: no single comparable pair; missing or multiple team stints prevent a summary ranking; Playoffs: no single comparable pair; missing or multiple team stints prevent a summary ranking. This describes team association, not an isolated player effect.

This position compares observed contributions, not innate ability. Offensive judgement uses PPG and TS; league-relative efficiency is a separate cross-era check. Playmaking uses assists per minute and assists/turnovers, not a complete model of creation. Defensive activity cannot settle individual defense. Team on/off is association rather than causation.

**Scope:** 1990-91–1990-91 versus 2014-15–2014-15; Regular Season, Playoffs.

## Key evidence

- **Offense and era / Regular Season:** Michael Jordan (1990): Points per game **31.46** per game, True shooting **60.5** %; LeBron James (2014): Points per game **25.26** per game, True shooting **57.66** %. [Evidence](https://stats.nba.com/stats/playercareerstats?PlayerID=893&PerMode=Totals&LeagueID=00) [Evidence](https://stats.nba.com/stats/playercareerstats?PlayerID=2544&PerMode=Totals&LeagueID=00)
- **Playmaking and ball security / Regular Season:** Michael Jordan (1990): Assists per 36 minutes **5.38** per 36 minutes, Assists per turnover **2.24** ratio; LeBron James (2014): Assists per 36 minutes **7.38** per 36 minutes, Assists per turnover **1.88** ratio. [Evidence](https://stats.nba.com/stats/playercareerstats?PlayerID=893&PerMode=Totals&LeagueID=00) [Evidence](https://stats.nba.com/stats/playercareerstats?PlayerID=2544&PerMode=Totals&LeagueID=00)

- **Follow-up: Completed.** Matched minutes, attempts and per-minute scoring are shown below. More PPG alone does not establish broader improvement.
- **What the follow-up changes:** LeBron James has higher playoff PPG but lower shooting efficiency. Minutes/game changed from 36.13 to 42.2, attempts/game from 18.54 to 27.2, and points/36 minutes from 25.17 to 25.64. This separates additional playing/shot opportunity from efficiency; higher PPG is not an across-the-board improvement.
